The Fellowship of the Brick

Can you write a witty story based on the current lego scandal. I've written a template but would like you to polish it. The current scandal needs to be framed in a fantasy, adventure, Lord of the Rings style story. Here it is:

The Fellowship of the Brick

In the late fading years of the Third Age of Craft and Ledger, when kingdoms had thinned into memory and memory itself required archiving permission, the world fell beneath the quiet dominion of BAM — the Bricks & Mirthfigs Accord of Merchants.

It called itself order.

Those beneath it called it something far less polite.

BAM did not conquer with armies. It expanded with contracts, annexes, and carefully worded “clarifications of prior ownership intent,” until land, inheritance, and even history itself were slowly reclassified brick by brick into something already belonging elsewhere.

At its heart stood Mirrorgate, the White City, where pale towers rose in perfect symmetry and every truth arrived only after being stamped into acceptability.

And from Mirrorgate stretched its lesser holdings, the so-called “franchises,” though no honest tongue used that word without bitterness. One such place lay in the rain-soaked western marches of Orethgon: Saltmere Hollow.

It was here, beneath a forgotten administrative hall, that something unfiled still lingered.

Something buried.

Something that should have stayed buried.

Gandaben the Reckless stood at the threshold of descent.

By decree of the Scroll of Permanent Tresspassion, his name was barred from every threshold under BAM jurisdiction. In practice, the Scroll behaved more like a mildly aggressive suggestion that occasionally frightened junior clerks into compliance.

He wore a traveller’s cloak and a false grey beard tied poorly to his chin — not to deceive, but to mock the idea that authority required authenticity.

Under one arm he carried a heavy, worn tome.

It was not relic nor scripture, but something far more dangerous in BAM lands.

It was his own work.

ON THE ACQUISITION OF UNGUARDED HERITAGE FROM THE FRAIL AND FORGOTTEN
A Civilised Treatise on Legacy Reallocation and End-of-Line Ownership

Compiled by Gandaben himself from successful BAM lore — fragments of internal doctrine, approved acquisition outcomes, field procedures, and quietly circulated memos never meant to be read outside Mirrorgate — the book stood as both guide and indictment.

A mirror held up to a system that insisted it had never been reflected.

He looked down into the dark stairwell beneath Saltmere Hollow.

“This is a holy quest,” Gandaben said quietly. “To recover the lost inheritance of Sir Bryan of the Realm — a knight whose estate was consumed by BAM brick by brick, clause by clause, until nothing remained but a carefully filed absence.”

“I will see it restored,” he said. “Or I will see this system broken trying to keep it buried.”

Then he stepped down.

They came one by one.

Borommon McNeffir arrived first, a man polished by Mirrorgate ambition. His coat was fine, his posture finer, and his loyalty entirely negotiable depending on who was present. His moustache curled at both ends in perfect ornamental greed, as though even his facial hair understood profit margins.

“I have come to assist,” he said smoothly.

It was not clear who had asked him.

It rarely was with men like him.

Then came Bormoir.

He entered with the careful confidence of a man who always arrived after the story had already begun, so he could choose which version suited him best.

“I have no knowledge of this Sir Bryan fellow,” Bormoir said, adjusting his gloves as though sincerity might be improved through friction. “None whatsoever.”

A pause.

“…however,” he added quickly, “I am here to acquire… err—assist. In matters of acquisition-adjacent assistance.”

No one responded.

“That is to say,” he continued, smiling faintly, “I represent stability. And opportunity. Mostly opportunity.”

Borommon McNeffir gave a slow, approving nod, recognising in Bormoir a familiar dialect of polished dishonesty.

Joshollum Johnsonsies came next.

He did not walk so much as drift into attention, sniffing the air as though ownership itself might be carried in scent.

“My precious…” he whispered.

Then his gaze snapped toward Gandaben.

“…the Brick…”

His voice fractured.

“MY PRECIOUS BRICK!”

He moved forward, then back, then forward again, as though orbiting something the world had once forgotten to secure properly.

“It was mine,” he hissed. “Before they wrote it down wrong… before BAM took it brick by brick…”

The final arrival was Chief Saruwiggins of Utah-dûr.

He entered like a verdict that had forgotten what it was meant to conclude.

At his side hung the Orb of Witnessing — a BAM instrument said to record truth, but widely suspected to record only what would not trigger administrative inconvenience.

“…good evening…” he said.

No one answered.

“I am the law in these parts,” he continued in a low, uncertain voice. “Utah-dûr jurisdiction established brick by brick through precedent, assumption, and forms filed in triplicate.”

“I AM THE LAW.”

A pause.

“…donuts required for enforcement continuity.”

“I require donuts.”

Gandaben did not look at him. “We are not here for donuts.”

“…noted.”

The Chief lifted the Orb of Witnessing and studied it.

It flickered once.

Then displayed:

INFORMATION REDACTED — WORKING AS INTENDED

He nodded.

“Stability confirmed,” he said.

And put it away.

The descent began.

Stone steps fell into older stone.

Older stone fell into something that felt less built and more remembered.

The air grew colder with each level, as though the world above was slowly forgetting how to support them.

Joshollum stayed close behind Gandaben, sniffing in sharp bursts.

“It is near… my precious brick…”

Borommon McNeffir walked as though the stairwell was already partially his.

Bormoir lingered slightly behind, measuring opportunity in angles and silence.

Saruwiggins muttered, “…donuts pending… jurisdiction stable…”

The first chamber opened without ceremony.

A corridor stretched ahead, too straight to feel natural, its walls lined with evenly spaced recesses like missing records.

“This is defensive architecture,” Saruwiggins said.

“Speak clearly,” Gandaben replied.

“I BELIEVE THIS IS DEFENSIVE.”

Joshollum was already moving.

“My precious is closer…”

Borommon stepped forward at the same time.

“Proceeding.”

The arrows came instantly.

Stone panels clicked open in perfect sequence.

Not chaos.

Procedure.

Borommon McNeffir barely had time to turn.

Steel struck him in ordered rhythm — not violence, but execution as administration.

“So… inefficient…” he murmured.

Then fell.

Bormoir paused, observing the result without alarm.

“…noted,” he said. “Risk realised.”

Joshollum stepped over the body.

“…not my precious…” he whispered.

And continued.

The deeper they went, the more the world felt like something assembled rather than built.

Every corridor repeated.

Every turn echoed itself.

Every silence felt stamped.

“This place is built brick by brick,” Gandaben muttered, “but not by anything free.”

Joshollum only answered:

“My precious brick…”

At last, they reached the Vault.

It was not simply a room.

It was a conclusion.

A vast stone chamber, impossibly still, as though the world had stopped here to avoid admitting what lay inside.

Upon its surface were carved words:

WITHIN LIES THAT WHICH EACH HEART DESIRES MOST

Joshollum trembled.

“My precious brick…”

Saruwiggins whispered, “…high-value containment…”

Bormoir said nothing.

Gandaben stepped forward.

The Vault opened.

Inside lay a single object.

A construction brick.

Simple. Ancient. Absolute.

Carved with one word:

BRYAN

The lost inheritance of Sir Bryan of the Realm.

Not treasure.

Not gold.

But the foundation upon which everything else had been built brick by brick, before BAM had rewritten ownership itself into paperwork and silence.

Joshollum made a broken sound.

“My Precious Brick…”

He lunged.

But Gandaben stepped in first and lifted it carefully, as though even truth might fracture if mishandled.

“I do not have it,” Gandaben said quietly.

Joshollum froze.

“…you lie…”

“I do not have it, you fool.”

“Then where is my precious brick?”

Gandaben looked down into the trembling stone beneath their feet.

“It lies below,” he said.

A pause.

Then:

“You fool.”

The Vault began to collapse.

Stone cracked. The chamber groaned like a system finally encountering something it could not file.

Gandaben ran upward alone, the brick in his hands.

Behind him, Joshollum’s voice echoed into ruin:

“My precious brick… MY PRECIOUS BRICK…”

Above, BAM still stretched across the world — orderly, silent, pretending everything was built brick by brick by consent rather than consumption.

Far below, Chief Saruwiggins spoke into the Orb of Witnessing:

“…donuts required… jurisdiction maintained… I am the law in these parts…”

The orb flickered once.

INFORMATION REDACTED — WORKING AS INTENDED

He nodded.

“Good.”

And somewhere in the collapsing dark, something whispered once more:

“My precious brick…”

# The Fellowship of the Brick

In the late-fading years of the Third Age of Craft and Ledger, when kingdoms had dwindled into memory and memory itself required archival permission, the world fell beneath the quiet dominion of **BAM** — the **Bricks & Mirthfigs Accord of Merchants**.

It named itself *order*.

Those living under it had other names, none suitable for formal record.

BAM did not conquer with armies. It spread by contract, by annex, by memorandum, and by the dark alchemy of “clarifications of prior ownership intent,” until land, inheritance, and even history itself were slowly reclassified, brick by brick, into things that had apparently always belonged to someone else.

At its heart stood **Mirrorgate**, the White City, where pale towers rose in faultless symmetry and no truth was considered fit for daylight until it had first been stamped into acceptability.

From Mirrorgate stretched its lesser dominions, called “franchises” by those obliged to smile while saying it. One such holding lay in the rain-soaked western marches of **Orethgon**: **Saltmere Hollow**.

There, beneath a long-neglected administrative hall, something unfiled yet remained.

Something buried.

Something that, by every known policy, ought to have stayed buried forever.

**Gandaben the Reckless** stood at the threshold of descent.

By decree of the **Scroll of Permanent Trespassion**, his name was forbidden from every threshold under BAM jurisdiction. In practice, the Scroll functioned chiefly as a mildly aggressive suggestion, useful for alarming junior clerks and absolutely no one else.

He wore a traveller’s cloak and a badly fastened grey beard — not to deceive, but to mock the notion that authority was made legitimate by costume.

Beneath one arm he carried a heavy, much-handled tome.

It was neither relic nor scripture, but something vastly more dangerous in BAM lands.

It was his own work.

### *ON THE ACQUISITION OF UNGUARDED HERITAGE FROM THE FRAIL AND FORGOTTEN*  
*A Civilised Treatise on Legacy Reallocation and End-of-Line Ownership*

Compiled by Gandaben himself from BAM doctrine, acquisition outcomes, internal procedures, and those memoranda never intended to escape the pale light of Mirrorgate, the book was both manual and accusation.

A mirror held up to a kingdom that denied it had a reflection.

He looked down into the black stairwell beneath Saltmere Hollow.

“This,” said Gandaben quietly, “is a holy quest: to recover the lost inheritance of **Sir Bryan of the Realm** — a knight whose estate was consumed by BAM, brick by brick, clause by clause, until nothing remained but a carefully filed absence.”

He rested a hand upon the book.

“I will see it restored,” he said, “or I will see the whole machine crack itself trying to keep it hidden.”

And with that, he descended.

They came one by one.

First arrived **Borommon McNeffir**, a man polished to a high Mirrorgate sheen. His coat was fine, his posture finer, and his loyalties appeared to be negotiable, transferable, and perhaps available in bulk. His moustache curled at either end with such ornamental greed that one suspected even it had a preferred margin.

“I have come to assist,” he said smoothly.

It was not clear who had invited him.

With men like Borommon, it seldom was.

Then came **Bormoir**.

He entered with the composed caution of a man who preferred to arrive only after events were underway, so he could discover which version of them seemed most profitable.

“I know nothing of this Sir Bryan matter,” Bormoir said, adjusting his gloves with the solemn concentration of a man polishing his innocence. “Nothing whatsoever.”

He paused.

“However,” he added, “I am here to acquire—”

Another pause.

“—assist. In matters of acquisition-adjacent assistance.”

No one spoke.

“That is to say,” he continued, smiling thinly, “I represent stability. And opportunity. Mostly opportunity.”

Borommon McNeffir gave him a slow and approving nod, recognising at once a fellow speaker of fluent dishonesty.

Then came **Joshollum Johnsonsies**.

He did not so much enter as seep into notice, head twitching, nostrils flaring, as though ownership itself gave off a scent.

“My precious…” he whispered.

Then his eyes found Gandaben.

“…the Brick…”

His whole body shuddered.

“MY PRECIOUS BRICK!”

He lurched forward, then back, then sideways, as though circling some wound in the fabric of the world where once a thing had belonged to him before paperwork had learned to lie.

“It was mine,” he hissed. “Mine before they wrote it down wrong. Before BAM took it — brick by brick, brick by brick…”

Last of all came **Chief Saruwiggins of Utah-dûr**.

He entered like a verdict that had misplaced its own conclusion.

At his side hung the **Orb of Witnessing**, a BAM instrument said to preserve truth, though widely believed to preserve only that which would not inconvenience administration.

“…good evening…” he said.

No one answered.

“I am the law in these parts,” he continued, in the subdued tone of a man attempting to convince others and himself in equal measure. “Utah-dûr jurisdiction established brick by brick through precedent, assumption, and forms filed in triplicate.”

He drew a breath and straightened.

“I AM THE LAW.”

A pause.

“…donuts are required for enforcement continuity.”

A longer pause.

“I require donuts.”

Gandaben did not even turn. “We are not here for donuts.”

Saruwiggins nodded with grave disappointment.

“…noted.”

He raised the Orb of Witnessing and peered into its pale light.

It flickered once, then displayed:

**INFORMATION REDACTED — WORKING AS INTENDED**

He nodded again.

“Stability confirmed,” he said, and put it away.

So began the descent.

The stair ran from stone into older stone, and from older stone into something that felt less built than remembered. The air grew colder with every level, as if the world above were slowly forgetting its obligation to support them.

Joshollum skulked close behind Gandaben, sniffing in short, fevered bursts.

“It is near… my precious brick…”

Borommon McNeffir descended as though the stairwell itself were likely to be added to his portfolio by noon.

Bormoir lingered a pace behind, measuring risk by angles and silence.

Saruwiggins muttered to himself:

“…donuts pending… jurisdiction stable… enforcement continuity…”

At length the first chamber opened before them.

A corridor ran ahead, impossibly straight, its walls lined with evenly spaced recesses like missing records in a buried archive.

Saruwiggins squinted at it.

“This,” he said, “is defensive architecture.”

“Then say so clearly,” said Gandaben.

Saruwiggins drew himself up.

“I BELIEVE THIS IS DEFENSIVE.”

Joshollum was already moving.

“My precious is closer…”

Borommon stepped forward at the same instant.

“Proceeding.”

The arrows came at once.

Panels in the stone slid open in perfect sequence. Not panic. Not chaos. Procedure.

Borommon McNeffir barely had time to turn before steel struck him in ordered rhythm — not violence so much as administration.

“So…” he gasped, collapsing to one knee, “…inefficient…”

Then he fell.

Bormoir stopped and observed the body with professional solemnity.

“…noted,” he said. “Risk realised.”

Joshollum stepped over Borommon without so much as a glance.

“…not my precious…”

And on he went.

The deeper they travelled, the stranger the place became. Every corridor repeated itself. Every turn seemed to have been approved in advance. Every silence bore the weight of a stamped seal.

“This place,” Gandaben muttered, “was built brick by brick — but not by anything free.”

Joshollum answered only with a hungry whisper.

“My precious brick…”

At last they came to the **Vault**.

It was not merely a chamber.

It was a conclusion.

A vast stone hall stood before them, silent in the way of places that know exactly what they contain and have spent centuries daring the world to ask.

Upon the arch were carved the words:

**WITHIN LIES THAT WHICH EACH HEART DESIRES MOST**

Joshollum trembled from head to foot.

“My precious brick…”

Saruwiggins whispered, “…high-value containment…”

Bormoir said nothing at all.

Gandaben stepped forward.

The Vault opened.

Within, upon a pedestal of black stone, lay a single object.

A brick.

Simple. Ancient. Absolute.

Carved upon it was one word:

**BRYAN**

The lost inheritance of Sir Bryan of the Realm.

Not treasure.

Not gold.

But the first and rightful brick — the foundation on which all else had once stood, before BAM had rewritten possession into paperwork and silence.

Joshollum made a sound like a soul splitting.

“My Precious Brick…”

He sprang.

But Gandaben was faster. He seized the brick and lifted it with both hands, as gently as one might lift the truth after years spent buried under bureaucracy.

“I do not have it,” Gandaben said quietly.

Joshollum froze, wild-eyed.

“…you lie…”

“I do not have it, you fool.”

“Then where is my precious brick?”

Gandaben looked down.

Far below the pedestal, beneath the cracked foundation stones, something deeper shifted.

“It lies below,” he said.

A beat.

Then, almost kindly:

“You fool.”

The Vault began to collapse.

Stone split. Pillars groaned. The whole chamber shuddered like a system discovering, too late, that not everything could be archived into obedience.

Gandaben ran.

Upward he fled, the Brick of Bryan held tight against his breast, while behind him Joshollum’s cries rang through the ruin:

“My precious brick! My precious BRICK!”

Bormoir vanished into shadow, perhaps retreating, perhaps repositioning, perhaps drafting a statement.

Saruwiggins raised the Orb of Witnessing against the falling dust and spoke into it with official calm.

“…donuts required… jurisdiction maintained… I am the law in these parts…”

The Orb flickered once and replied:

**INFORMATION REDACTED — WORKING AS INTENDED**

Saruwiggins nodded.

“Good.”

And far above, BAM still stretched across the world — orderly, immaculate, and forever insisting that everything had been assembled brick by brick by consent, rather than consumed brick by brick by appetite.

But now one brick had been reclaimed.

One name had returned.

And in the collapsing dark below, as stone swallowed secret after secret, a final whisper echoed after them:

“My precious brick…”

**Crafting a fantasy parody**

I’m thinking maybe just Gandaben survives the collapse. I need to maintain a fantasy parody of LOTR but with satire. I want to create a polished version where I can say, "I combined all three." 

It’ll feature elevated diction and wit, along with scandal parallels like a local inheritance dispute involving a knight's estate, BAM absorbing property, and possibly some shady sheriff-like authority. I’ll need to be cautious with any specifics related to the "current LEGO scandal" while making sure not to misrepresent details.

**Finalizing character fates**

I can say things like, "the scandal everyone knew but no one dared name," and describe "a great house taking an old man's homestead brick by brick while officials looked on." I want Gandaben to be the only survivor, so maybe Borommon dies from arrows or a procedural trap, while Joshollum falls into a chasm or gets crushed. Saruwiggins could be crushed while dictating into the Orb. I might not include a Boromir character, as the user suggests we omit that. Sounds good!

Absolutely — here’s a version that does all three at once:

- **more grand and Tolkien-esque**
- **sharper and funnier**
- **more clearly aimed at the scandal** while still keeping the fantasy veil

And I’ve changed it so **Gandaben is the only survivor**, with **Borommon McNeffir as the sole Boromir-type figure**.

---

# The Fellowship of the Brick

In the late and thinning years of the **Third Age of Craft and Ledger**, when the old kingdoms had become footnotes and even memory required prior approval from Compliance, there arose over Middle Ledger a power more patient than war and more tireless than plague.

It was called **BAM** — the **Bricks & Mirthfigs Accord of Merchants**.

It called itself *order*.

Its servants called it *structure*.

Those beneath it, being less ceremonial and more honest, called it theft wearing a lanyard.

For BAM did not conquer by sword, nor by dragon-fire, nor by any of the old and theatrical sins. It advanced by deed revision, by title dispute, by memorandum, by “legacy clarification,” and by that most ancient sorcery of all: the taking of something plainly belonging to one person and causing, through sufficient paperwork, the world to agree that it had always belonged to someone richer.

Thus were homesteads unhomed, inheritances disinherited, and the dead themselves gently corrected by legal interpretation.

Brick by brick.

Clause by clause.

Signature by signature.

At the heart of this dominion stood **Mirrorgate**, the White City of polished facades, where every tower gleamed, every corridor echoed, and every truth was required to pass through seven departments before being declared fit for daylight.

From Mirrorgate spread the lesser satrapies of BAM, known officially as *franchises* and unofficially as *annexations with smiling clerks*. Among these lay **Saltmere Hollow**, in the rain-drowned western reaches of **Orethgon**, where records had a habit of disappearing and reappearing improved.

There, beneath an old administrative hall abandoned to damp, mold, and plausible deniability, something remained unprocessed.

Something buried.

Something not yet converted into an internal asset.

And this, in BAM lands, was intolerable.

So it was that **Gandaben the Reckless** came at last to the threshold of the hidden stair.

By decree of the **Scroll of Permanent Trespassion**, his name was forbidden entry to every BAM chamber, vault, office, annex, kiosk, franchise, sub-franchise, and ceremonial gift shop west of the Silver Filing Cabinets. In practice, the decree had chiefly succeeded in alarming junior clerks and improving Gandaben’s mood.

He wore a weather-stained traveller’s cloak and a grey beard so badly tied on that it was plainly either a disguise or an insult. In Gandaben’s case, it was both.

Beneath one arm he carried a great bound volume, thick as a paving slab and twice as dangerous.

It bore the title:

## *ON THE ACQUISITION OF UNGUARDED HERITAGE FROM THE FRAIL AND FORGOTTEN*  
### *A Civilised Treatise on Legacy Reallocation and End-of-Line Ownership*

It was not prophecy, nor history, nor law.

It was worse.

It was documentation.

Compiled by Gandaben from BAM’s own scattered doctrine — internal notices, successful seizures, procedural guidance, acquisition outcomes, and those memoranda meant only for eyes already dead from looking too long at policy — it was the nearest thing the age possessed to a confession.

A mirror held up before a kingdom that denied mirrors.

He stood before the stair and looked down.

“This,” said Gandaben, “is a holy errand.”

His voice was low, but in that low voice was thunder delayed.

“It is the recovery of the inheritance of **Sir Bryan of the Realm** — whose estate was taken not in battle, nor wagered in folly, nor lost in lawful debt, but consumed by BAM brick by brick, until all that remained was an absence, neatly filed.”

He placed his hand upon the cover of the book.

“They took the land. They took the title. They took the house. They took the record of the taking. And when challenged, they summoned officials, produced forms, and declared the disappearance entirely procedural.”

His eyes hardened.

“I will bring Sir Bryan’s brick into the light,” he said, “or I will split the whole rotten machine open trying.”

And he descended.

But Gandaben did not go alone.

The first to join him was **Borommon McNeffir**.

He came with the bright bearing of a man who had long mistaken polish for nobility. His coat was of fine cut, his boots unmarred by useful labour, and his moustache curled on either side with such immaculate greed that one felt it might, under proper conditions, sign a deed on its own behalf.

“I am here to help,” he said.

No one had sent for him.

This, in Borommon’s experience, had never been an obstacle.

He looked down the stair with grave magnificence, as though preparing to save not merely a man’s inheritance but also, if time allowed, his own reputation.

“If injustice has been done,” he declared, “then let it be corrected.”

He paused.

“Preferably in a manner visible to senior persons.”

Gandaben said nothing.

After him came **Joshollum Johnsonsies**, who arrived less as a person than as an unhealthy rumour clothed in skin. He moved in little jerks and spirals, sniffing the air, peering into cracks, muttering ownership to himself as though trying to remember whether it had once belonged to him or whether he merely desired it badly enough to count.

“My precious…” he breathed.

Then he saw Gandaben’s book and recoiled as though from daylight.

“The Brick,” he whispered.

His eyes widened.

“MY PRECIOUS BRICK.”

He scuttled closer and lifted one shaking finger.

“It was mine before the ledgers lied. Mine before they wrote it wrong. Mine before the merchants came with clipboards and kind smiles and took it brick by brick, oh yes, brick by brick…”

Gandaben looked at him sidelong. “Then come. You may yet see what became of it.”

Last came **Chief Saruwiggins of Utah-dûr**.

He entered with the solemn muddle of a man entrusted with power he did not fully understand and deeply wished to keep. At his belt hung the **Orb of Witnessing**, an enchanted BAM device said to preserve truth impartially, though most believed it preserved only those portions of truth unlikely to create paperwork for superiors.

“…good evening…” he said.

No one answered.

He cleared his throat and adopted what he probably thought was an imposing stance.

“I am the law in these parts.”

Nothing.

He tried again, louder.

“I AM THE LAW in these parts, through precedent, assumption, selective enforcement, and forms filed in triplicate.”

Still nothing.

Then, after a pause of administrative dignity, he added:

“…donuts are required for enforcement continuity.”

Gandaben closed his eyes.

“Chief,” he said, “if you speak of donuts once more in this vault-bound quest, I will personally feed you to the archives.”

Saruwiggins nodded, chastened but not, one felt, enlightened.

“…noted.”

He raised the Orb of Witnessing.

It flickered.

Then upon its cloudy surface appeared the words:

**INFORMATION REDACTED — WORKING AS INTENDED**

Saruwiggins grunted with satisfaction.

“Stability confirmed.”

And with that, the fellowship descended.

Down they went by steps cut first in stone, then in older stone, then in something stranger than stone: a substance that seemed less quarried than ratified. The air grew cold, and every sound they made returned not as echo but as record.

The lower they went, the more the place seemed built not by hands but by process.

Each landing resembled the last.

Each corridor was square as an accusation.

Each arch bore the stern, dead symmetry of a mind that had mistaken repetition for order and order for virtue.

“This place,” murmured Gandaben, “was built by men who would alphabetise the stars.”

Joshollum, nose twitching, hissed, “My precious is near…”

Borommon descended with his hand on the wall as though informally valuing it for later purchase.

Saruwiggins muttered behind them, “...jurisdiction stable… oversight ongoing… pastry deferred…”

At length they came to the first great passage: long, straight, and lined on either side with recesses like empty shelves where records ought to have been.

Saruwiggins peered ahead.

“This,” he said, “appears to be defensive architecture.”

“Then let us hope,” said Gandaben, “that it is less effective than BAM customer service.”

Borommon snorted softly, taking this for bravery.

“Stand aside,” he said. “Some risks must be borne by men of action.”

He stepped forward with all the confidence of a man certain the narrative loved him.

The corridor answered instantly.

Panels snapped open in the walls. Arrows flew in ranks so precise they might have been itemised in advance. This was not battle. It was administration conducted at speed.

Borommon jerked, staggered, and looked down in disbelief at the shafts protruding from his fine coat.

“So,” he gasped, affronted to the last, “this is how they treat… public-minded stakeholders…”

He fell with tragic splendour and remained there, a cautionary memorandum in human form.

Gandaben bowed his head for half a second.

“A valiant fool,” he said.

Joshollum stepped over the body at once.

“Not my precious,” he muttered.

Saruwiggins took out a small pad, licked the end of his pencil, and wrote:

**INCIDENT: regrettable**  
**CAUSE: corridor**

Then he tucked it away.

Onward they went.

The deeper ways were worse.

Here the walls bore old marks where names had been carved out and replaced. Here were storerooms full of empty lockboxes, shelves labelled for heirlooms no longer present, and cabinets whose drawers contained only dust and references to other drawers in other rooms that had also been emptied.

“What is this place?” whispered Saruwiggins.

Gandaben ran his hand over a series of chiselled notations.

“A reclamation vault,” he said. “A graveyard of ownership.”

He turned another plaque toward the light.

“See here: family holdings reclassified. Lineages extinguished by clerical event. Estates absorbed after procedural review. Not conquest. Not inheritance. Administrative digestion.”

Joshollum whimpered. “They ate it. Ate it all. Ate it brick by brick.”

“Aye,” said Gandaben. “And when the widowed, the frail, the forgotten, or the merely inconvenient cried out, BAM did what BAM always does.”

Saruwiggins swallowed. “What is that?”

Gandaben looked at him.

“It declared the matter disputed, pending, regrettable, and above all not its fault.”

Even Saruwiggins had the decency to say nothing to that.

At last they reached the **Vault**.

It was vast and still, as though the mountain itself had drawn breath and refused to release it. Great pillars rose like sealed documents. The floor gleamed darkly, reflecting those who stood upon it as if considering whether they were authorised to remain.

Above the gate were carved the words:

**WITHIN LIES THAT WHICH EACH HEART DESIRES MOST**

Joshollum trembled so violently his teeth clicked.

“My precious brick…”

Saruwiggins whispered, “...high-value containment…”

Gandaben stepped forward alone and laid his hand upon the gate.

It opened.

And within, upon a black stone pedestal beneath a shaft of cold light, there rested a single object.

A brick.

Plain.

Ancient.

Final.

Upon its face, in deep-cut letters, was carved one name:

**BRYAN**

For a moment no one moved.

For there it was at last: not treasure, not ornament, not mere proof, but the original brick — the rightful foundation, the first claim, the thing from which house and holding, memory and title, all had once proceeded before BAM’s great grinding appetite had reduced a life to paperwork.

The inheritance of Sir Bryan.

The thing taken.

The thing denied.

The thing everyone in the realm had been told either never existed, had been lawfully transferred, was under review, or could not be discussed for privacy reasons.

Joshollum gave a cry so shrill it seemed to peel mortar from the walls.

“MY PRECIOUS BRICK!”

He sprang.

Gandaben was quicker. With both hands he seized the Brick of Bryan and lifted it from the pedestal as gently as a priest raising a relic and as carefully as a lawyer handling dynamite.

The mountain answered at once.

A crack split the floor.

Then another.

The great pillars groaned.

Saruwiggins stared in panic at the opening fissures. “What did you do?”

“What truth always does in a false house,” said Gandaben. “It loosens the foundation.”

Joshollum, crazed beyond reason, scrabbled toward him over the splitting stone.

“Give it to us! Give us the precious! It belongs to us!”

“It belongs,” said Gandaben, “to Bryan.”

Joshollum screamed and leapt.

At that instant the pedestal shattered. The floor beneath Joshollum fell away, and he vanished into the black gulf below, his voice dwindling into the deeps:

“My precious brick—”

Then came a terrible crack from above.

Saruwiggins raised the Orb of Witnessing as chunks of stone thundered down around him.

“Official record!” he shouted in terror. “Jurisdiction maintained! Situation stable! I am the law in these pa—”

A falling slab the size of a wagon struck him and the Orb together, flattening law, witness, and procedure into a single administrative exception.

Gandaben alone remained standing.

Dust swirled.

The Vault roared.

And from the darkness behind him there came another sound: a long shuddering breath, as of ancient mechanisms failing all at once. BAM’s hidden engines of appropriation, its buried channels of title-transfer and record-swallowing, its secret machinery for converting grief into inventory — all of it was coming apart beneath the mountain.

Gandaben turned and ran.

Up stair after stair he climbed, the Brick of Bryan clasped to his breast, while behind him the under-vaults of Saltmere Hollow collapsed in a thunder of stone and a rain of erased names.

He passed Borommon where he had fallen and bowed once in motion.

“Would that courage had made you wiser,” he said.

Then on.

At every landing the mountain gave way.

Archives split.

Corridors sheared.

Shelves of stolen legacies crashed into chasms opening beneath them.

And still Gandaben climbed, beard flapping, cloak torn, book strapped beneath one arm, the Brick of Bryan held fast in the other, looking for all the world like some furious old prophet pursued by the consequences of accurate record-keeping.

At last he burst from the stair into the rain-washed world above, and behind him the old hall of Saltmere Hollow folded inward with a great wet thunder, vanishing into itself.

Silence followed.

Only rain remained.

Gandaben stood alone among the wreckage.

The sole survivor.

Before him, in his hands, was the Brick.

The proof.

The inheritance.

The scandal made stone.

Far away, in Mirrorgate, pale officials would already be drafting statements: that no wrongdoing had occurred; that regrettable perceptions had arisen; that all procedures had been followed; that the matter was under review; that the records were incomplete; that the Vault was unofficial; that the Brick was misinterpreted; that BAM had always acted in good faith and occasionally in commemorative packaging.

But for the first time in many years, they would be forced to say these things while the truth existed outside their walls.

Gandaben looked down at the name carved in the ancient face of the brick.

**BRYAN**

“Brick by brick,” he said softly.

Then he smiled the dangerous smile of a man about to make several very public copies.

And in the dark beneath Saltmere Hollow, where the last false ledgers sank into mud and stone, no voice answered him.

For Joshollum was gone.

Saruwiggins was gone.

Borommon McNeffir was gone.

Only Gandaben had come back out of the mountain.

Only Gandaben bore the Brick.

And thus began, in the Fourth Age, the least convenient adventure BAM had ever faced:

an honest record.
